prompt: Why is the output of `filter.py` 6 by 6, when the digit is 8 by 8?
hint: Count where a 3-pixel window can stand.

choices.text: The filter drops the blank border of the digit
choices.why: The size has nothing to do with the ink: a full image would give 6 by 6 as well.

choices.text: A 3-wide window fits in 6 places across 8 pixels
choices.why: Right. It can start at columns 0 to 5; starting at 6 it would need a column 8 that does not exist.

choices.text: PyTorch halves the size of every convolution's output
choices.why: Halving would give 4, and the loops in NumPy gave 6 before PyTorch was called.

choices.text: Its stride is 2
choices.why: The loops move one pixel at a time; with stride 2 and no padding the answer would be 3.

prompt: With the filter `[[-1, 0, 1]] * 3`, the third column of the output runs from -5 to -34. What is under the window there?
hint: The filter subtracts its left column from its right one.

choices.text: A blank part of the image
choices.why: Blank on both sides gives zero, as in the last column's top rows.

choices.text: The left edge of the stroke, where ink begins
choices.why: That is the first column, 21 to 48: more ink on the right than on the left gives a positive sum.

choices.text: The right edge of the stroke, where ink ends
choices.why: Right. Ink on the left and blank on the right makes the subtracted side win.

choices.text: A part inked evenly from side to side
choices.why: Even ink cancels, left against right, and gives a number near zero.

hint: Look at the third line about the dot.

choices.text: Moved two pixels, it crossed into the next block and the output moved
choices.why: Right. Pooling tolerates a shift inside its block, and no more.

choices.text: Nothing: the output stayed `[1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]` for every shift
choices.why: At a shift of 2 it printed `[0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]`.

choices.text: Average pooling ignores shifts and max pooling does not

choices.text: Max pooling ignored the dot, which is why nothing changed
choices.why: It kept the dot: the 1.0 is the dot's value, carried into the block's output.

prompt: `nn.Conv2d(1, 16, kernel_size=3, padding=1)` has 160 parameters on the 8 by 8 digits. How many does it have on 64 by 64 grey images?
hint: What does a filter depend on?

choices.text: 10,240, because the image has 64 times as many pixels
choices.why: That would be true of a dense layer, which pays per pixel. A filter does not.

choices.text: 160, the same
choices.why: Right. The same 16 filters slide over any size of image; weight sharing is the saving.

choices.text: 1,280, because it needs eight times more filters to cover the width
choices.why: The number of filters is the 16 written in the layer; the image size does not change it.

choices.text: It cannot run on that size without being rebuilt
choices.why: A convolution runs on any height and width; only the input channels must match.

choices.text: The same 3 by 3 place in all 16 maps of the first layer

choices.text: 16 different places of a single map
